# Analysis to prefer

### Number of variables :

61 variables to describe people's opinion on politics, 58 variables on environment, including two that are already in the first dataset (idno and region).=> lots of variables : could be useful to do a PCA as the variables are correlated, or a selection of variables with ridge (lasso would not perform well here).

SO even though the number of variables is high, it is still smaller than n.

## Variance-bias trade-off :

Many observations (2582), but representing a very wide population (European population in largely urban areas, near capitals).

### Response variable :

The problem is that our response variable is in fact several variables right now. We should find a way to summarize the information we have into one variable (response variable).
Or choose only one variable. In this case, the best one is probably lrscale (on left-right scale ).

### Type of variable :

We have mostly ordered variables (scale from 1 to 5), and a few categorical variables (country, region). Some stat learning techniques do not perform well with ordered variables. Linear/logistic regression should be avoided. Regarding the 

### Goal :

We want to be able to analyze the relationship between the variables, to interpret it rather than to predict.

## Methods :

We could do one PCA with linear regression and compare the efficiency with another method that is good for inference and doesn't assume linearity (mse comparing). We would need another way to select the variables then (best subset selection, or simply applying a ridge or lasso (but lasso bad with correlated data)).

# PCR

## Least-Square Regression

Does it have to be linear ? Apprently yes. p.267 ISLR

To keep in mind :
 As more principal components are used in the regression model, the bias decreases, but the variance increases.
 PCR will tend to do well in cases when the first few principal components are sufficient to capture most of the variation in the predictors as well as the relationship with the response.
 While the supervised dimension reduction of PLS can reduce bias, it also has the potential to increase variance, so that the overall benefit of PLS relative to PCR is a wash
 
Let's follow the steps in the ISLR book 
```{r}
library(pls)
set.seed(4423283)
```

```{r}
head(envdf)
```

Problem with missing data :
We need to delete them. Especially for the outcome variable.

```{r}

```
I finally got it to work, with scale=TRUE !!
With  this code the variables are scaled to have the same variance, and a 10-fold cross validation is computed. Let's note that here the variables are not treated differently whether they are ordinal or numerical.

The Root mean squared error stays approximately the same over the number of components, but reaches a minimum around 28 components (between 20 and 30 at least.)

```{r}
pcr.fit
```

Maybe we should divide the dataset into a training and test datasets :

```{r}
length(envdf_clean$idno)*0.8
```


```{r}
set.seed(4423283)
train_size = 1724
train_ind = sample(seq_len(nrow(envdf_clean)),
    size = train_size
  )
train_set = envdf_clean[train_ind, ]
test_set = envdf_clean[-train_ind, ]
```


```{r}
pcr.fit2 = pcr(lrscale~.-1, data = train_set,scale=TRUE, validation="CV") # using region too
summary(pcr.fit2)
```

```{r}
validationplot(pcr.fit2, val.type = "MSEP")
```
Interesting enough, using region we then get a clear number of components needed. We need 13 components.

We could try one pcr with 30  variables (lower RMSE) and 98.9% of variance explained, and one with 3 PC, with 57.37% variance explained.
```{r}
pcr.pred <- predict(pcr.fit, data=test_set[,-3], ncomp = 3)
 mean((pcr.pred - test_set$lrscale)^2)
```

```{r}
pcr.pred <- predict(pcr.fit2, data=test_set, ncomp = 13)
mean((pcr.pred - test_set$lrscale)^2)
```

## Other analysis to compare it with (classification):

- Multinomial logistic regression ? Interpretation possible, but regarding the baseline chosen (reference group in dependent variable)
-GLM (with appropriate link function like logit or probit)
-QDA -> plus flexible, biais plus faible mais variance plus élevée car prend en compte des relations non-linéaires. Doesn't matter with the size of our dataset, the variance can stay low. The model can adapt itself enough to the real relationship thanks to the large sample size, and it's easier to reduce the variance than the bias. Also, QDA is assuming that the observations
from each class are drawn from a Gaussian distribution and that each class has its own
covariance matrix. (could be seen with boxplots). QDA better than KNN to deal with larger nb of features + easier to interpret.

The ndy variables are number of days => not a scale. The aqiw ones are scales. We can sum them up based on the day to have an idea of the air quality per day instead of per component.
Those are the only ordinal variables.


## Let's apply PCA (over all the dataset):

```{r}
envdf_clean$aqiw2 = envdf_clean$aqiw2d + envdf_clean$aqiw2dno2 + envdf_clean$aqiw2dpm10 + envdf_clean$aqiw2dpm2_5 + envdf_clean$aqiw2do3 # five instead of 6 in the codebook because the last one was taking only one value
envdf_clean$aqiw = envdf_clean$aqiwd + envdf_clean$aqiwdno2 + envdf_clean$aqiwdpm10 + envdf_clean$aqiwdpm2_5 + envdf_clean$aqiwdo3

# Then we can set the initial ones to 0

envdf_clean = envdf_clean[,-c(4:13)]
head(envdf_clean)
```


```{r}
pr.out = prcomp(envdf_clean[,-c(1:3)], scale = TRUE) # no scaling because the variables are already scaled
pr.out
```

```{r}
summary(pr.out)
```

### Cumulative PVE

```{r}
cumul_prop_var_expl = summary(pr.out)$importance[3,]
plot(cumul_prop_var_expl~c(1:43), type="b", ylab="Cumulative PVE", xlab="Number of Principal Component", pch=16, main="Cumulative explained variance")
abline(h=0.9, col="red")
```
Looks like we get what we want at 11.
```{r}
cumul_prop_var_expl
```


### Ratios 

```{r}
cumul_prop_var_expl = summary(pr.out)$importance[3,]
nElem=length(cumul_prop_var_expl)
ratios=(cumul_prop_var_expl[2:(nElem-1)]-cumul_prop_var_expl[1:(nElem-2)])/
(cumul_prop_var_expl[3:nElem]-cumul_prop_var_expl[2:(nElem-1)])
ratios
```

```{r}
nComponents_selected = which.max( ratios[-c(40:41)] ) + 1
nComponents_selected
```
We would select 39 principal components in our analysis. (insane)

### Cattell's scree plot

```{r}
plot(pr.out, type="l", main="Scree plot of the PCA")
```
As Cattell suggests looking at the last significant drop to select the number of components, we could here decide to keep 3 components. After 3 components, the variance do not differ strikingly.


### Velicer's MAP

```{r}
library(EFA.dimensions)
# Velicer's Map
MAP(envdf_clean[,-c(1:3)], corkind='pearson', verbose=TRUE)
```
According to the Velicer's MAP, 8 components should be kept.

### Horn's parallel analysis

```{r}
library(nFactors)
ev = eigen(cor(envdf_clean[,-c(1:3)]))
ap = parallel(subject=nrow(envdf_clean), var=ncol(envdf_clean)-3, rep=1000)
nS = nScree(x=ev$values, aparallel=ap$eigen$qevpea)
plotnScree(nS, main="")
```
We would keep 9. So overall, we should keep between 9 and 11 variables.
Let's keep 13 and rotate :

```{r}
library(GPArotation)
ob = oblimin(pr.out$rotation[,c(1:20)])
ob
```


pr.out$rotation gives 60x20
pr.out$x gives 2000x20
to get 2000x60 standardize matrix, we need ...
ob$loadings is 60x20
Then to get the values with rotation (2000x20) we need 

```{r}
data_cent = pr.out$x %*% t(pr.out$rotation)
pr_x_rot = data_cent %*% ob$loadings
pr_x_rot
```

Okay ! So now we want it as a dataframe with region and lrscale.

```{r}
new_df = as.data.frame(pr_x_rot)
new_df$region = envdf_clean$region
new_df$lrscale = envdf_clean$lrscale
```

```{r}
head(new_df)
```

